cd7f2193ad: Build00:20–00:55 Getting the right hand ready
3968918e5f: Strum from the wrist and keep the arm steady
9234360c91: Pick angle: its centre line points the same way as your index finger and thumb, with 2–3 mm of tip showing
12cc8e2523: Wrist like shaking off water: the elbow stays fixed as the pivot, and the relaxed wrist swings up and down
9d815ad068: Strum range: downstrokes go from the lowest string you need to string 1; upstrokes hit only the top 3 or 4 treble strings
ce6dc74736: Touch: tilt the pick slightly so it brushes the strings; the sound is rounder and the pick is less likely to catch or drop
88b8a15a9f: Strum from the thick strings toward the thin ones
b768b852c6: From the thin strings toward the thick ones, treble strings only
e63f771fc9: The hand still swings but stays off the strings
1a633c9cc1: Remember one rule: the hand never stops swinging. Down, up, down, up, like a clock's pendulum; whether it touches the strings is what changes the rhythm.
73e3f4be32: BuildPart 2: Strum marks used in Chinese-language books
d8f09204e9: Learn these three marks before reading Chinese guitar music
5159da87dd: Pluck down on the bass strings, for example strings 5, 4 and 3 for a C chord
b1ddae5126: Strum down on the treble strings, for example strings 3, 2 and 1
0e7a6d72e4: Strum up on the treble strings, strings 1, 2 and 3
0cc4852ee0: Some Chinese-language books draw arrows following "the strings on the page", the opposite of Western books. When you get new music, find the key first.
8badab4ba5: Arrows always show the hand's direction: ↓ toward the floor, ↑ toward the ceiling. Chapter 5's "boom-chick-chick" uses X.
876a47a850: Quarter notes: one strum per beat, with the hand coming back up on the half beat
7397e74393: Hollow arrows are ghost strums: the hand goes back up and stays off the strings.
ed33f01298: Strong, weak, medium, weak: that's the 4/4 groove.
e3fa3be09e: 8 beats: the upward stroke makes a sound too
adfa22afc1: The ghost strum from before now touches the strings: down up down up, eight even strokes
cff7386aab: Slightly heavier downstrokes and lighter upstrokes give it shape
5e8d905094: Choose "Open strings" first to practise just the right hand, then switch to "C G Am F" once you're steady
88bc5d9b45: Start at 60 BPM and only speed up after two steady rounds in a row
3489d2972b: Hide a beat: a tie moves the accent forward
6ae7170639: Syncopated folk rock: beat 3 is taken by a tie
46fcae81a8: The sound on the second half of beat 2 is tied into beat 3. Beat 3 isn't strummed, so the usual "strong, weak, medium, weak" is broken up and it sounds lighter and more driving.

7b3d1c3a0c: Three small tricks for great-sounding strumming
29e57f058f: Rest your left-hand fingers lightly on the strings and stay relaxed; strumming gives a percussive "chk chk", perfect for practising the right hand on its own.
434e73aa64: Downstrokes a bit heavier, upstrokes a bit lighter. When strumming syncopation, make the upstroke in "down-up" clear and the syncopated feel appears.
68ed3c6557: Strum only the strings you need
564330bf6e: C and Am start from string 5, F from string 4; only G uses all six. A clean bass makes a clear chord.
1013eb6c42: Why upstrokes hit only the treble strings
5a21bea17a: An upstroke starts from string 1, so the hand naturally touches only the first three or four strings. Brushing the treble lightly works like a drummer's hi-hat, setting off the heavy downbeats.
600f60f7ec: 16 beats: each beat splits into four, and your hand swings twice as fast
ebfff77f15: Say "1 e & a" on each beat. "1" and "&" go down, "e" and "a" go up, following the same rule as 8 beats.
3c8bbce6bc: The original handbook's rule: keep downstrokes on the beat and add variety on the offbeats. The groove is still "strong, weak, medium, weak", with finer detail and more drive.
9ada84f726: 16 beats at 60 BPM means your hand swings as fast as 8 beats at 120 BPM. Keeping up at 50 BPM today is a great result.

2023d9d447: MythStrumming too hard makes the pick catch or drop and slows the beat. A relaxed wrist gives a crisp sound.
aeccec1bd1: On a ghost strum, your hand can stop and rest
84c34a1973: MythIf your hand stops, the next stroke will be late. A ghost strum means "keep swinging, stay off the strings".
4a19378263: Upstrokes should hit all six strings
80e64e935e: MythUpstrokes only need to brush the top 3 or 4 treble strings.
d7e578e1bb: Strumming comes mainly from the wrist
8e0326d485: FactThe elbow is the pivot and the wrist does the swinging; big arm swings tire you out quickly.
ed90831780: Syncopation means leaving out one stroke
fce9812532: FactThe stroke that's left out is on beat 3, so the accent moves forward and the groove changes with it.
ddfe8df8f1: A metronome gets in the way of practice
4fb4265cc8: MythIf it feels like it's in the way, your beat isn't steady yet. Slow down first, then catch up with the metronome.
